Honestly, I have a gaming group that would really like this game.  I can see how the impromptu story telling genre doesn't appeal to everyone, but there is a large crowd out there that loves games on the more casual side.  Games where there are no points, stats, min-maxing, resource management, or moving pieces; where the entirety of the game stems from using your imagination and where "winning" or "losing" is completely overshadowed by having some laughs with your buddies.

Some of the most gut-busting moments with my gaming group have come from games like "Say Anything" or "Snake Oil" where you're making stuff up and not so much playing the game as you are playing the player by appealing to their interests and sense of humor.  I love those sorts of experiences, and while it's fun to sit down with a dense game of Arkham Horror or a strategic round of 7 Wonders, some nights we just want to sit around and use our wit to create dumb scenarios to laugh about.

Again, I get it; this style of game is not for everyone, and a lot of people likely look in on these games and think "What's the point?"  It's true that the experience definitely relies on to how close you are with your gaming group, what style of humor they have, their general creativity, and everyone's general mood, but I think that these sorts of games have a place at the table.  You certainly need to be willing to accept that there is no clear cut winner or loser, and even if there was, it doesn't matter at all.  What matters is getting some friends gathered around the couch, having some drinks, and laughing your asses off.

GSF's release was lackluster for me with all of the fiddling and typos, and Tactics is impressive but not my favorite.  BattleCon is awesome but came in an unwieldy, disorganized, and inefficient box for its expansion with Legacy.

Friends, have you actually PLAYED Pixel Lincoln?  You have to shuffle SECTIONS of a deck repeatedly and there are at least three different mechanics for conveying power up items in a sidescrolling Mario-esque world.  It's just my opinion...but if anyone thinks Sentinels Story War is the first instance of >G backing a subpar product, then I'd have to label you "uninformed".  Play Pixel Lincoln and get back to me.

The point is that I'm excited for the opportunity to show kids in my life something I love without expressing the difference between "put into play" and "played", or the differences between damage immunity, reduction, prevention, or redirection.  I'll wait and see what happens with this new Kickstarter, because Pixel Lincoln would've shaken me out of this company if I had a one-strike rule.

Fortunately the sprite art is great in Pixel Lincoln.  Unfortunately that doesn't make it A FUN GAME.

If you think I'm being somewhat off topic when talking about PL, I've at least played it.  I'll give Story Wars a try once before I start impotently shouting at the sky and claiming Greater Than Games have sold their souls to Mammon, the God of filthy lucre and terrible crowdfunded games.

My frustration has nothing to do with it being a bad/good game. It has everything to do with how SotM was handled, and how this is being handled. GtG made a decision about how they wanted to released the story and lore for these characters. Many of us look at all the pictures, flavor text, and come here every day because we love the lore and characters. Nothing wrong with this.

However, SotM does have a specific target audience, an audience that doesn't mesh with their other Multiverse products, and this is what is frustrating me. The choice not to give out the story outright, but to add in more hints in products that won't appeal to the SotM gamer. I have Tactics just for the added story elements that I didn't want to miss. It rarely gets played because of the groups I am in. Tactics isn't so bad becuase of the 5-year gap, but there is still a lot of info.

This trend seems to be going with Story War. I don't think It will get played a lot, since not everyone is a Sentinels fan, and I have better party games. Yet, if I want to know more of the story that has been hidden and secreted away, I have to buy a product I might never use. This is what is frustrating me.

WIth SotM, I have everything, not just because I want to support the company or being a completionist, but because I want to see the entire story that GtG wants to tell. In recent months, my resolve to do this have lessened drastically. Besides picking up Tactics, I then had to pick up the Video game to get a card, donate to a worthy cause to get another, and now pick up a new game I might never play.

I will admit that a lot of this is just me, and how I want everything, but the frustation is still there. GtG has chosen its style of storytelling, and how to distribute the story. For the first few years this worked fine, and everything was isolated to SotM the card game, but we still don't know the story, and we are needing more and more ways to get tidbits.

If you take a look at Tom's video, he doesn't say that it is a bad game. He says it is a story-telling game with its inherent strengths and weaknesses. However, he does say that there is no point in getting the game. You can have a better and more creative experience by giving everyone an index card and writing down whatever characters they want. There simply isn't enough in the box to warrant a purchase. 

That being said, you could play Sentinel Conflicts right now using the cards that you have (just get opaque sleeves). Even if you didn't want to mix the cards, you could just order some form the store and play now, instead of in June. The only thing you are missing is the art, and this is what frustrates me. I could get the experience of the game right now, but I would be missing the art. Essentially, that is all the game has for me: more art and story. Now, If I want to know that story, I have to buy more stuff that I don't need.

So, what does GtG do? They finally give us the story straight out, but couple it with the game. I actually love this dichotomoy. The KS has a product that finally, actually, tells the official story with a product that encourages you to do what you want. The book is $25, but you can save on shipping if you get both. Add on to this that there are no stretch goals for the books, and it feels like that GtG finally gives us what we want, in order to use it for something we might not. (I am not saying this is what is being done, but it is how it feels).

Now, if the book was being advertised as a way to learn some basic story for people new to the Multiverse and want to play Story War, I get that, I would still be upset, but I get it. However, there is nothing that indicates this is their approach. Which forces me to ask the question: who is this game for?

As I mentioned above, you have a lot easier time creating stories with the Story War base game, because most people know about those characters. If someone has no idea about the Multiverse characters, what exactly will they do? More importantly, will someone who has knowledge of the game want to play with them? I hope so, but I think it is a harder sell. It definitely feels like the game is being targeted to players of SotM, but therein lies the problem.

I hope the KS does well, and it looks like it will fund. However, the hardcore SotM fans (and GtG fans) are not entirely onboard. Both here and on BGG, the comments have been very negative. Nothing wrong with branching out and getting more people, but it shouldn't be at the cost of the current fans.

posts.cooked:
Thanks for the feedback everyone, whether you like the idea of Sentinel Conflict or not! I expected that there would be a thread like this when we launched the Kickstarter, and I am glad that it has proceeded in a civil manner :) Here are my answers to some of the questions that came up in this thread:

Q) Who is "Story War: Sentinel Conflict" for?

A) It is for:

*Fans of party/story telling games who want to play one with comic book heroes.

*Fans of Sentinel Comics who want to play a story telling game with characters they love.

*People with casual/non-gamer friends who they want to introduce to Sentinel Comics and eventually convince to play SotM or Tactics.

*Parents who want to introduce Sentinel Comics to their young children.

*Fans of Sentinel Comics who really want a bunch of small art prints with new character art.

 

Q) Why is GTG splitting up the story of Sentinel Comics across multiple different games?

A) We love the world of Sentinel Comics, and believe that there are a few different types of game that work very well with the stories of that universe and, if possible, we would like to make those games and through them tell more stories from Sentinel Comics. Each game is going to appeal to a different core audience, though there will be a lot of overlap.

However, we realize that people are also invested in the story and will want to stay up to date with it. That was one of the motivating factors behind setting Tactics at a different point in the Sentinel Comics timeline; the stories of SotM and Tactics are related, but distinct. With Sentinel Conflict, the game does not provide critical advancement to either story, or contain its own story arc. Instead, it acts as an introduction to the characters and world of Sentinel Comics. We don't want anyone to feel like they have to buy it just for the story.

 

Q) Why did GTG choose Story War as the basis for this party/story telling game?

A) We have played a number of party/story telling games with the "subjectivity mechanic" (popular examples including Apples to Apples and Cards Against Humanity), and we believe that Story War is the best of the genre. (On an amusing note, the back of the original Story War box actually has a quote from Max Tempkin, creator of Cards Against Humanity, saying that Story War is better than CAH). In addition, we felt that the characters, locations, and items format translated very well to the Sentinel Comics universe.

Games and hobbies thrive on impulse buys.  People buying a game because they really, really want it and people who buy a game because they really, really want to buy a game don't make much of a difference when it comes to sales.  How the players react to the game may be quite different, of course, but if someone is so disinterested in the game that they don't want to throw fifteen to twenty bucks at it when it's bundled with a comic they really want, then they're voting with their dollars.  I've sold plenty of SotM sets at the FLGS I work at, but I don't really differentiate whether the buyer was really interested in superheroes, co-op games, card games, or anything else.  I tell them it's a great superhero co-op game, describe some of the mechanics, and then they buy it or they don't and I see what else they my be interested in.  That curiosity of "was this an impulse buy or a calculated, deliberate purchase," is rampant in this field, and it could be applied to nearly any game when someone has some cash burning a hole in their pocket.

Of course this doesn't have much bearing on the quality of the game, but I don't know that it matters much if people are getting it just to have it.  If they get it and it isn't their thing they took a calculated risk and didn't really lose out on much because their expectations weren't high.  If they got it because they really wanted it and they didn't get what they wanted then that's way more disappointing.

Hello, fans and friends of the Multiverse.

We have learned a lot from Kickstarter over the years. During the Kickstarter for the Shattered Timelines expansion for Sentinels of the Multiverse, we said we would not run any more Kickstarters for Sentinels of the Multiverse products - that game is well established enough to support its own expansions. Since then, we have decided to go a step further and not run Kickstarter campaigns for expansions for any existing products. If a product is strong enough to warrant an expansion, it shouldn't need a Kickstarter campaign to make that expansion happen. 

When we run Kickstarter campaigns, the purpose is two-fold: procure funding for a product we are interested in making and gauge interest in said product. As a result - even though we are cancelling the Kickstarter for Sentinel Conflict and the Cosmic Contest comic book - we consider this Kickstarter campaign to have successfully done its job. It let us know whether we should make these products or not.

We had hoped there would be interest in a Sentinel Comics version of Story War, as we had played and enjoyed Story War. However, the response here, on our website and others, and on social media has been clear: Story War is not a direction people are interested in seeing the Multiverse go. Good to know! We are glad to have learned that now and not after printing several thousand copies of the game.

We were more surprised by a general lack of interest in the comic book. "When are you going to start making actual comic books?" is a question we get with great regularity, and so we were excited to answer "NOW!" with this campaign. And when we were asked for a digital version, we figured out what we needed to do to make PDFs of the comic available as pledge levels. However, here we are, most of the way through the campaign, with barely over a hundred backers of the comic book levels. This Kickstarter has also informed us that, though people may be interested in reading comic books from Sentinel Comics, few are interested in purchasing them. And that is good to know. We are still interested in making comic books, and Adam and I will continue to work on them, but they will remain side projects at most, as we have to continue to make actually salable products to continue to survive as a company.

The other feedback that we have gotten from this campaign is just how much people want us to continue making content for the Sentinels of the Multiverse card game and for the Sentinel Tactics tabletop game. That is great! Those of you interested in Sentinels of the Multiverse should check out our recently released Challenges and Achievements! Also, you will be excited to learn that the Wrath of the Cosmos expansion hasbegun shipping, so if you preordered it, you'll get it soon! And if not, it'll be available for sale soon! Sentinel Tactics fans can look forward to more official Sentinel Tactics Tournaments! And gaming events are happening all over the place this month as part of Multiverse Month! Get your local gaming store involved!

Additionally, keep an eye on our website, as we will have even more exciting news about the world of Sentinel Comics in the next few weeks. The cancellation of this Kickstarter is a somber event, but what we have learned from it is invaluable, and we look forward to giving you more of the game content you want!

Thank you for being a part of our Multiverse. We couldn't do this without you. Keep on saving the Multiverse

-Christopher Badell
Game Design Director
Greater Than Games, LLC

Even counting everyone who pledged for the comic + game, there was not enough interest in the comic to justify the cost of production. The reason for this is that not only is there infrastructure, etc, necessary to make something like that, but comics are also incredibly time consuming from both an art and a writing standpoint. We wanted to know if it was worth it from an economic perspective to invest that time, and it turns out it probably isn't, which is really good to know!

Obviously I don't know the actual numbers for >G, but in general the actual cost of the product is 25% of the retail price. Say they've paid $5 for the game from the manufacturers. They'll sell it to retailers/distributors at wholesale, which is about $10. Someone has to be paid wages to package up a batch of games for each retailer. Marketing costs money. Profit per game out of the $5 that's left? Not very much, I imagine.

If they sell the game directly, they have to pay someone to package each individual game (more per game than withe the bulk order). They also have to advertise, deal with returns/replacements, buy/maintain equipment and storage, etc… and if you're expecting them to pay $10 for your free shipping, that remaining $5 isn't going to go very far to cover that. Let's say they make $2.50 per game if they pay for shipping (I'm making up the numbers, and I don't believe it would be as high as that) - they'd have to sell FIVE TIMES as many games to make the same profit as NOT paying for shipping. Unlikely to happen.
